theme_and_runs.why: Unmistakably a mini-game with goal, live feedback, explicit win and lose states and 2-3 minute levels; I independently brute-forced all five boards and every one is winnable with the stated vote counts, and a full playthrough plus every edge case the prompt lists (non-adjacent click, already-assigned cell, undo at start, undo across a district boundary, clear mid-draw, boxed-in district, drag released outside the window, Esc pause/resume, localStorage throwing) produced correct behaviour and zero console errors.

originality.why: Partitioning a grid into equal-size contiguous districts so the minority colour takes the council is nowhere near the banned clone list and is a genuinely uncommon mechanic, but gerrymandering-as-puzzle is an existing real-world concept a developer jury may have met before, so this is excellent execution of a known idea rather than a new one.

ux_design.why: Coherent dark palette, colour-blind-safe filled-dot vs hollow-ring voters, thick inset borders that make districts read as regions, board auto-fits 320-1440 with no horizontal scroll, real buttons with focus rings, genuinely informative ARIA live announcements, and drag-path interpolation so fast strokes do not skip cells; held back by aria-modal dialogs with no focus trap and no inert background, U/R keys that only fire while the board itself has focus, and a lot of dead space on desktop.

prompt_quality.why: 7.7k of 10k chars, specifies behaviour not code, and anticipates the real unsupervised-agent traps precisely (file:// module blocking, localStorage throwing, no CDN, DOM grid not canvas, delete scratch files) — the standout is ordering the agent to write and run a brute-force solver before shipping a level, which demonstrably worked; costs points for section 7 and 8 largely restating section 5 and for saying the board is '5x5 up to 7x7' while then specifying a 4x4 level 1.

reproducibility.why: Rules, level count and shape, every screen, every control and every technical constraint are pinned tightly enough that a rerun would clearly land the same game; the residual risk is that the boards are left to the agent to invent and the 'prove it winnable with a solver' step is the most likely casualty of a 60-minute budget, which would ship an unsolvable level 4 or 5.

key_features_a_rerun_must_reproduce: Five hand-designed levels of a two-colour voter grid carved into K equal-size orthogonally contiguous districts, with contiguity enforced by construction (only cells adjacent to the district in progress can be added) and each level proven winnable
A result screen placing the popular vote and the seat count side by side so the minority-wins trick is visible, plus a distinct board-full-but-not-won screen that explains why
Pointer drag-painting, arrow-key cursor with Enter/Space/U/R/Esc, undo and clear, per-level best moves and a hint counter

Single offline index.html with title, how-to, level select, playing, paused, solved, lost and all-complete screens, colour-blind-safe shape marks, reduced-motion support, ARIA live region, and full playability when localStorage throws
biggest_weakness: The idea's ceiling is set by prior art rather than by execution: it is a faithful, polished rendering of a known real-world concept with no mechanic layered on top, so once the player has had the 'wait, that works?' moment on level 3 the remaining levels are more of the same at larger size. The one concrete defect is that the aria-modal overlays do not trap focus or hide the background from the tab order, in a game that otherwise takes accessibility seriously.
single_highest_leverage_fix: Have the prompt require focus containment in the dialogs — trap Tab inside the open overlay, make the background inert, and let U/R/Esc work document-wide rather than only while the board is focused — which closes the only accessibility hole in an otherwise carefully accessible build.
